chapter.name: Temperature and its Measurement
chapter.blurb: Touch alone cannot reliably judge hotness or coldness; temperature is the reliable measure, read with a thermometer. Clinical thermometers measure body temperature (normal ~37.0 degrees Celsius); laboratory thermometers measure a wider range and have a range and a smallest readable division; three scales (Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin) express temperature, with Kelvin as the SI unit; room thermometers and weather reports track air temperature.

scope_in.item: Our sense of touch cannot always reliably judge whether a body is hot or cold, shown by the three-container hand-dipping activity
Temperature is a reliable measure of the hotness or coldness of a body; a hotter body has a higher temperature; a thermometer is a device that measures temperature
Two main kinds of thermometers: clinical (for human body temperature) and laboratory (for other purposes); digital clinical thermometers and non-contact/infrared thermometers

Normal human body temperature is taken as 37.0 degrees Celsius (an average, not an exact universal value), normally staying between 35 degrees Celsius and 42 degrees Celsius; armpit readings run about 0.5 to 1 degree Celsius lower than actual body temperature; digital thermometers are replacing mercury ones because mercury is toxic

Three temperature scales: Celsius (degree Celsius, C), Fahrenheit (degree Fahrenheit, F) and Kelvin (kelvin, K, the SI unit); 37.0 degrees Celsius equals 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit; unit-writing conventions (capitalised scale names, space between number and unit, no plural 's' on symbols, no degree sign with K)
Converting Celsius to Kelvin using Temperature in kelvin = Temperature in Celsius + 273.15; absolute zero is close to -273.15 degrees Celsius (0 kelvin), the lowest possible temperature

Structure of a laboratory thermometer: a sealed glass tube with a liquid-filled bulb, a Celsius scale marked along it, and a liquid column that rises or falls with temperature; the liquid is generally alcohol or mercury

A thermometer's range is the span from its lowest to highest measurable temperature (e.g. -10 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees Celsius); the smallest readable division is found by dividing the temperature gap between two bigger marks by the number of small divisions between them

Correct technique for a laboratory thermometer: bulb not touching the container, held vertically without tilting, eye level with the liquid column, reading taken while still immersed since the column falls once removed; temperature stays constant while water boils or ice melts

Room thermometers give an approximate idea of room temperature; weather reports state a day's maximum and minimum air temperature, which vary day to day due to weather factors and generally rise towards summer and fall towards winter

concepts.name: Hot or cold: touch versus temperature
concepts.description: Touch alone cannot always reliably judge hotness or coldness; temperature is a reliable numerical measure of it, read using a thermometer.
concepts.idea: Our sense of touch is not always a reliable way to judge hotness or coldness; temperature is a reliable numerical measure of how hot or cold a body is.
concepts.rule: A hotter body has a higher temperature than a colder body; the difference in temperature tells us how much hotter one body is compared to another; a device that measures temperature is called a thermometer.
concepts.example: In the three-container activity, a hand that was in warm water feels the same lukewarm water as cool, while a hand that was in ice-cold water feels the identical water as warm.

concepts.name: Temperature scales: Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin
concepts.description: Temperature can be stated on three scales -- Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin (the SI unit) -- and converted between Celsius and Kelvin using a simple formula.
concepts.idea: Temperature can be expressed on three scales: Celsius (degree Celsius), Fahrenheit (degree Fahrenheit) and Kelvin (kelvin, the SI unit); a given temperature has an equivalent value on each scale.
concepts.rule: 37.0 degrees Celsius equals 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit; Kelvin temperature = Celsius temperature + 273.15; absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, is -273.15 degrees Celsius (0 kelvin). Scale names are capitalised; unit symbols are capital letters with a space before them, and K never takes a degree sign.
concepts.example: A fever of 101 on the Fahrenheit scale is about 38.3 degrees Celsius, a genuine fever, whereas 101 on the Celsius scale would be impossible for a living human body.

This works because Kelvin's zero point (absolute zero) is at -273.15 degrees Celsius, so any Celsius value is 273.15 units above that starting point when expressed in kelvin.
s: States a clear, usable memory trick
Correctly identifies that you add (not subtract) 273.15
Explanation correctly connects this to absolute zero's position

Since the same physical temperature can look very different depending on the scale used (for example, 37 degrees Celsius is 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit), '20' and '68' could actually be very close in real hotness if one is in Celsius and the other in Fahrenheit, since 20 degrees Celsius is about 68 degrees Fahrenheit; without knowing the units, no safe comparison can be made.
s: States the assumption is not safe/questionable
Explains this using the idea that scales can make the same temperature look different
Notes correctly that 20 degrees Celsius and 68 degrees Fahrenheit are actually close

s: Names all three scales correctly

concepts.name: Laboratory thermometer: structure, range and smallest division
concepts.description: A laboratory thermometer's readable span is its range, and its precision is set by its smallest division, found by dividing a bigger gap by the number of small divisions in it.
concepts.idea: A laboratory thermometer is a sealed glass tube with a liquid-filled bulb at one end and a Celsius scale marked along its length; the liquid column rises or falls with temperature.
concepts.rule: A thermometer's range is the span from its lowest to its highest markable temperature; its smallest readable division is found by dividing the temperature difference between two bigger marks by the number of small divisions between them.
concepts.example: If the gap between the 0 and 10 degree Celsius marks is divided into 10 small divisions, each division reads 1 degree Celsius; with 50 divisions between 0 and 100 degrees Celsius, each division reads 2 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Explain why two thermometers can have the same range but different smallest readable divisions.

questions.q: Design a simple activity, different from the one in the book, that a classmate could use to determine both the range and the smallest division of an unfamiliar laboratory thermometer they are given for the first time.
questions.a: Sample: First, read the lowest and highest numbers marked on the thermometer to state its range. Then, pick any two neighbouring bigger marks, count how many small divisions lie between them, and divide the temperature difference between those two bigger marks by that count to get the smallest division.

concepts.name: Correct technique for measuring temperature with a laboratory thermometer
concepts.description: A laboratory thermometer must be held vertically, kept away from the container's sides, read at eye level, and read while still immersed for an accurate result.
concepts.idea: Using a laboratory thermometer correctly requires immersing the bulb fully without touching the container, holding it vertically, and reading it while it is still immersed.
concepts.rule: The eye must be level with the liquid column while reading; the reading must be taken while the bulb remains immersed, since the liquid column starts falling as soon as the thermometer is removed.
concepts.example: A student who lifts the thermometer out of the water before reading it will get a lower, incorrect reading because the liquid column has already begun to fall.

s: Poster content includes correct vertical, non-touching placement

Poster content includes at least one additional correct precaution

concepts.name: Air temperature: room thermometers and daily maximum/minimum
concepts.description: Room thermometers give an approximate idea of a room's temperature; weather reports state daily maximum and minimum air temperature, which vary and follow seasonal trends.
concepts.idea: Room thermometers give an approximate idea of the temperature of a room; weather reports state the day's maximum and minimum air temperature.
concepts.rule: Air temperature varies from day to day depending on weather, and generally rises approaching summer and falls approaching winter; recording daily maximum and minimum temperatures over many days lets you analyse a temperature trend.
concepts.example: A 10-day weather record might show air temperature gradually rising as summer approaches, with the daily maximum always higher than the daily minimum for that same day.

questions.q: Explain why a single day's maximum and minimum air temperature readings are not enough to conclude that a season is changing.
questions.a: A single day's readings can be affected by short-term or unusual weather events, so one day is not enough evidence of a lasting trend; recording temperature over many successive days lets a real pattern, rather than a one-day fluctuation, be analysed.

questions.q: A news anchor says, 'Yesterday was 35 degrees Celsius and today is 36 degrees Celsius, so summer has clearly arrived.' Evaluate this claim using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: This claim is not well supported by just two days of data. Air temperature varies daily due to many factors, and only recording data over a longer period, such as 10 successive days, and observing a genuine, sustained rise can reasonably suggest that summer is approaching; a one-degree change between two days could simply be normal day-to-day variation.
s: States the claim is not well supported by only two days of data

Notes that a longer record would be needed to properly support the claim

questions.q: Design your own simple weather-tracking project, different from the one described in the book, that a class could carry out over a month to study how air temperature changes with the season. Describe what you would measure, how often, and what you would look for in the results.
questions.a: Sample: Each school day at the same time, record the outdoor air temperature using a room-style thermometer placed in a shaded spot, along with the date, for one full month. At the end of the month, plot the readings on a simple line graph against the date and look for whether the temperature is generally rising, falling, or staying about the same, which can indicate whether the season is changing.
s: Describes a clear measurement plan (what, how, how often)
Plan runs over a reasonable extended period suitable for detecting a trend
